planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio plant in coarse, fast-draining orchid bark mix in bright, indirect light; Sharry Baby orchid cannot tolerate frost and is grown outdoors year-round only in zones 10-11.

directions: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio plant in coarse, fast-draining orchid bark mix in bright, indirect light; Sharry Baby orchid cannot tolerate frost and is grown outdoors year-round only in zones 10-11. One of the most widely grown Oncidium-alliance hybrids, it produces tall, branching sprays of dozens of small, deep maroon-red to chocolate-brown flowers edged in white, famous for an intense fragrance that many growers describe as smelling exactly like chocolate or vanilla, strongest on warm, sunny mornings. Vigorous and free-flowering compared to many orchid hybrids, it blooms readily under bright windowsill or greenhouse conditions and is a favorite for its combination of showy, long-lasting flower sprays and genuinely pleasant scent. Water when the bark mix approaches dryness, feed lightly with a balanced orchid fertilizer during active growth, and repot every one to two years once the bark breaks down.

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio plant in a well-drained, moisture-retentive orchid mix in bright, indirect light; Redvale zygopetalum prefers cooler conditions than many tropical orchids and appreciates protection from intense heat.

directions: Grow as a houseplant or shaded patio plant in a well-drained, moisture-retentive orchid mix in bright, indirect light; Redvale zygopetalum prefers cooler conditions than many tropical orchids and appreciates protection from intense heat. Bold, waxy flowers combine mottled green-and-brown-striped sepals and petals with a strikingly veined, deep purple-red lip, produced in upright spikes with an intense, sweet fragrance often compared to hyacinth that fills a room. Unlike many orchids, zygopetalums prefer to be kept consistently moist rather than allowed to dry out fully between waterings, more like a typical houseplant than a dry-loving epiphyte, and they respond well to regular feeding during active growth. Provide bright indirect light, keep the mix evenly moist, and give plants a slightly cooler rest with reduced water after flowering to encourage strong rebloom.

planting.note: Grow as a shaded, cool, humid houseplant or greenhouse specimen in a fine, well-drained orchid mix; Veitch's masdevallia is a cool-growing Andean cloud-forest species that struggles in hot, dry conditions and is best suited to an air-conditioned room or shaded, humid greenhouse.

directions: Grow as a shaded, cool, humid houseplant or greenhouse specimen in a fine, well-drained orchid mix; Veitch's masdevallia is a cool-growing Andean cloud-forest species that struggles in hot, dry conditions and is best suited to an air-conditioned room or shaded, humid greenhouse. Brilliant, glowing orange-red, triangular flowers with a fine, iridescent, shimmering texture rise on slender stems above a low tuft of leathery leaves, a color and shine so vivid that it was noted by nineteenth-century orchid hunters as one of the most striking flowers in the Peruvian Andes. Native to high-elevation cloud forests, it requires consistently cool temperatures, high humidity, and constant air movement, making it a challenging but rewarding species for growers able to replicate cloud-forest conditions rather than a plant for an average warm home. Keep the mix constantly moist but never soggy, and avoid any temperature above the mid-80s Fahrenheit, which stresses and can kill the plant.

common_name: Watch Chain Crassula (Rattail Crassula, Zipper Plant)

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or xeriscape container in bright light to full sun in fast-draining, gritty cactus-and-succulent mix; watch chain crassula stores water in its tightly packed leaves and rots quickly if left in soggy soil.

directions: Grow as a houseplant or xeriscape container in bright light to full sun in fast-draining, gritty cactus-and-succulent mix; watch chain crassula stores water in its tightly packed leaves and rots quickly if left in soggy soil. Tiny, scale-like, bright to yellow-green leaves are stacked in four tight, overlapping columns along thin, upright-then-trailing stems, giving each stem the look of a braided cord, zipper, or chain of tiny watch links, an unusual, almost architectural texture unlike typical rounded succulent leaves. Native to dry regions of southern Africa, it is easy and fast-growing, tolerating bright light, drought, and general neglect, and it branches and spreads readily to fill a container or rock garden pocket with its distinctive braided stems. Water only when the soil is fully dry, propagate easily from stem cuttings allowed to callus before potting, and provide bright light to keep growth compact rather than stretched.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America reference

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant, hanging basket, or xeriscape container in bright light to full sun in fast-draining, gritty succulent mix; dwarf trailing kalanchoe wants good drainage and rots in constantly moist soil.

directions: Grow as a houseplant, hanging basket, or xeriscape container in bright light to full sun in fast-draining, gritty succulent mix; dwarf trailing kalanchoe wants good drainage and rots in constantly moist soil. Small, scalloped, silvery-gray leaves dusted with a fine, powdery farina cover trailing, woody-based stems, and clusters of small, bright pink-purple, star-shaped flowers appear in late winter and early spring, standing out against the soft silver foliage. Native to dry, rocky slopes in Madagascar, it is a compact, low-water succulent well suited to a hanging basket, rock garden pocket, or the edge of a raised xeriscape bed where its trailing habit can spill over an edge. Handle the powdery leaves gently, since the farina rubs off easily, and water only when the soil is fully dry.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America reference

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded xeriscape container in bright indirect light to partial sun in fast-draining, gritty succulent mix; bicolor ox tongue tolerates lower light than most succulents and rots in overly wet or dense soil.

directions: Grow as a houseplant or shaded xeriscape container in bright indirect light to partial sun in fast-draining, gritty succulent mix; bicolor ox tongue tolerates lower light than most succulents and rots in overly wet or dense soil. Thick, tongue-shaped, dark green leaves marked with irregular pale green to white bands and spots are arranged in two opposite rows in juvenile plants before spiraling in maturity, and tall, arching flower stalks bear clusters of small, pink-and-green, pouch-shaped flowers that give the genus its stomach-referencing name. Native to South Africa, it tolerates the lower, indirect light of a shaded windowsill or porch better than most succulents, making it a good choice for spots too dim for cacti or echeverias but still too bright and dry for typical foliage houseplants. Water only when the soil is fully dry and divide offsets from the base to propagate.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America reference

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded xeriscape container in bright, indirect light in fast-draining, gritty succulent mix; cushion aloe scorches in direct hot sun and rots in dense or constantly wet soil.

directions: Grow as a houseplant or shaded xeriscape container in bright, indirect light in fast-draining, gritty succulent mix; cushion aloe scorches in direct hot sun and rots in dense or constantly wet soil. Plump, translucent-tipped leaves are densely packed into tight, low rosettes, with the swollen, window-like leaf tips allowing light to filter down into the plant's interior, an adaptation shared with several small haworthias native to rocky crevices in South Africa where the rest of the plant hides below ground level for protection from intense sun. Its small, clustering rosettes spread slowly by offsets into a dense mat, making it well suited to a shallow succulent dish garden, terrarium-adjacent display, or windowsill collection where its unusual translucent leaf tips can be appreciated up close. Water only when the soil is fully dry, provide bright but indirect light, and separate offsets to propagate or refresh a crowded pot.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America reference

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or xeriscape container in bright light to full sun in fast-draining, gritty cactus-and-succulent mix; Lola echeveria holds its best pastel color and tightest rosette form in bright light and rots quickly in wet soil.

directions: Grow as a houseplant or xeriscape container in bright light to full sun in fast-draining, gritty cactus-and-succulent mix; Lola echeveria holds its best pastel color and tightest rosette form in bright light and rots quickly in wet soil. A popular hybrid between Echeveria lilacina and E. 'Perle von Nurnberg,' it forms a tight, perfectly symmetrical rosette of smooth, powdery, pale lavender-pink leaves with a soft, almost pastel glow that intensifies in bright light and cooler temperatures. Its compact size and refined coloring make it a favorite for succulent arrangements, wedding favors, and mixed containers, and it offsets readily to form small clusters over time. Water only when the soil is fully dry, avoid wetting the leaves to protect their delicate powdery coating, and provide bright light to prevent the rosette from stretching and losing its tight form.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America reference
